title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
statement:
Given a string `s`, return the length of the longest **substring** (a contiguous block of characters) in which no character appears more than once.

A subsequence that skips characters doesn't count. The empty string has answer `0`.
constraints: s consists of printable ASCII characters: letters, digits, symbols and spaces

target.note: O(1) space because the alphabet is fixed at 128

hints: Suppose s[lo..hi] has no repeats and s[hi+1] is already in it. Do you need to start again from lo + 1, or do you know exactly how far lo has to move?

Keep a window [lo, hi] with no repeats and grow hi one character at a time. Remember the last index of every character (a HashMap, or an int[128] for ASCII). When s[hi] was last seen inside the window, jump lo to just past that index.

For each hi: lo = max(lo, last[s[hi]] + 1). The max matters: an old occurrence to the left of lo must not pull the window backwards (try "abba"). Then store last[s[hi]] = hi and update best = max(best, hi - lo + 1).
followups: Why do you need max(lo, …) when jumping? Give an input that breaks without it.
What changes if s can contain any Unicode character?
Generalise: the longest substring with at most k distinct characters.
explain: Slide a window [lo, hi] that never contains a repeat. Advance hi one step at a time, and keep the most recent index of each character in an int[128] (a HashMap<Character, Integer> works for any alphabet). If s[hi] was last seen at position p ≥ lo, the window can't include both, so set lo = p + 1. Taking max(lo, p + 1) stops a stale occurrence from moving lo backwards, which is what "abba" tests. Record hi - lo + 1 after each step. Each index enters the window once and lo only ever moves right, so it's O(n) time and O(1) space for a fixed alphabet. The HashSet version that removes from the left one character at a time is also O(n), since every character is added and removed at most once. Restarting the scan from every index is O(n · alphabet).
